rationale: B wins because it keeps the three real stories and refuses the padded one. A's "AI matchmaking just went mainstream" asks one Bumble relaunch to carry a whole category trend it cannot prove; B correctly kills that as "No facts about any other dating app were supplied." B's "Bumble's AI relaunch is a turnaround bet with no numbers yet" is the sharpest frame here because it turns the missing post-relaunch paying-user data into the story instead of pretending the comeback is already working.
gaps_in_A: "AI matchmaking just went mainstream" is overreach. One Bumble relaunch does not prove AI matchmaking is mainstream or a "category-standard feature" without evidence from other dating apps.

"her first fix is AI" and "first major public move" are plausible but not supplied. The update says the founder returned this year and the relaunch is happening, not that this is her first fix or first major move.

"Bumble's brand promise is that its message-first model empowers authentic connection" decorates the facts. The update gives women-message-first and user criticism of AI as inauthentic; it does not supply Bumble's own authenticity promise.
"the relaunch is the company's public answer to the falling stock price" assigns motive too confidently. Better: investors will judge whether the relaunch can answer the user and stock decline.
gaps_in_B: "by the company's own position" is too cute. The facts say post-relaunch paying-user trend is not yet reported; they do not say Bumble framed that absence itself.

"the market is pricing it before any post-relaunch paying-user data exists" is directionally fair for a public company, but it needs stock movement, analyst notes, or trading context before becoming a hard claim.
The next step names "journalist-fit-check" before there is a journalist. The practical next move is pick the angle, build a shortlist, then fit-check individual names.
